band_rule.name: empirical_p10_p90
band_rule.reading: In 80% of past five-year periods (50 states and DC, forecast origins 1990-2015) the actual permit total fell inside this band; on 2016-2020 forecasts, 98%. It is a statement about history, not a probability.
band_rule.applied_to_counties: The ratios come from state totals and are applied to every county; a single county's past errors are larger.
band_rule.reading_history: Coverage was 56% at origins 2005-2010, the bust, and 75% at 2011-2015, the recovery, against 89% to 98% in other periods; a band fitted on history does not foresee a turn in the market. Refitted each year on closed windows only, the band covered 61% of 2000-2020 runs and under 5% at origins 2005-2008.
band_rule.alternative: see the 20-year swing range (Adam Ruege's rule), shown separately

alternative_band.name: adam_20yr_swing
alternative_band.credit: Rule from Adam Ruege's Housing Reform Estimator v2.0 (a teammate's prototype).
alternative_band.how_built: Point = permits in 2021-2025. Low and high stretch it by the state's own slowest and fastest five-year totals of 2006-2025, each divided by their average.
alternative_band.how_it_did: Rerun on past years, the actual total fell inside in 181 of 255 state forecasts (71%) and in 87% of 2016-2020 forecasts; its high end was typically 2.44 times its low end. The headline band: 98% and 2.97 times.
alternative_band.why_not_headline: It is narrower, but it makes no fixed promise about how often it holds, and it missed 31 of 51 states for the five years after 2005. It was tested with its own starting point, so it is shown exactly as tested, beside the headline rather than mixed into it.
narrative: Another way to draw the range, from a teammate's earlier prototype: start from New Hampshire's 2021-2025 permits (24,200) and stretch them by the state's own slowest five years (2009-2013, 0.67 times the 2006-2025 average) and fastest (2021-2025, 1.31 times): 16,200 to 31,600.

Rerun on past years, the actual total fell inside in 181 of 255 state forecasts (71%) and in 87% of 2016-2020 forecasts; its high end was typically 2.44 times its low end. The headline band: 98% and 2.97 times.

baseline.method: Mean of 2023-2025 Census BPS units authorised (estimates with imputation), by county and structure type, x 5.
narrative: If current rules continue, New Hampshire would permit about 24,300 homes over 2026-2030: the 2023-2025 average carried forward 5 years.
In 80% of past five-year periods the actual total fell between 0.54 and 1.59 times this kind of estimate, which here means 13,000 to 38,600; that is a range from history, not a probability.
Rockingham County accounts for 27% of the total, and single-family homes make up 63% of it.

housing_units_pep.label: Census housing-unit estimates: net change since April 2020
housing_units_pep.measure: July 1 estimate of the latest year minus the April 1 2020 estimates base
housing_units_pep.caveat: These estimates are built partly from building permits, so they are a consistency view, not an independent measurement of homes added.
narrative: Census housing-unit estimates put New Hampshire's housing stock at 662,160 in July 2025, 23,400 more than in April 2020 (+3.7%).
These estimates are built partly from building permits, so they are a consistency view, not an independent measurement of homes added.

adu.label: Accessory dwelling units by right
adu.formula: ADUs completed = detached homes x tier rate x 5 years; increment = that x newly affected share x ramp; permits = increment x HCD permits per completion

benchmark.interpretation: What California cities with similar home values completed, transferred to this state's detached homes; it does not subtract what current rules already produce.

conversion.text: Completed ADUs x California HCD permits per completed ADU (two-year lag, 1.18 at mid): some permits are never built, so a completed ADU stands for more than one permit.

current_law.note: Three of the four benchmark features are in New Hampshire law in every town with zoning: one ADU per lot, attached or detached, of at least 600 square feet. The fourth, no added parking, is not: towns may require one more space. So 3 / 4 = 0.75 of the benchmark is already in law and 0.25 would be newly affected. Towns may also still require the owner to live on site.

assumptions: Assumptions selected for this calculation; legal rights and the time needed to build still need local evidence.
